name: open-ALERT
tagline: A configurator for ALERT and ALERT2 flood-warning sites: say what a site must do, see the hardware that fits, its costs and consequences.
about: For anyone planning ALERT or ALERT2 field stations, repeaters or base stations. Each site goes from needs to requirements to hardware picked from a 263-part catalogue (open and closed, Raspberry Pi to industrial), then to a bill of materials, a power budget with battery and panel sized, labour and running costs, and the consequences of the choices. The Network tab adds sites up and checks that what field stations send, repeaters relay and bases receive actually meet. A static page with no server: state lives in the browser and in share links. The base station builder (build.html) goes deeper on a receiving base running RPi ALERT: how it fits together physically and in the code, which computer keeps up with how many channels, the SDR mounting, a bill with price ranges, lead times and suppliers, and the build steps.

status.summary: The hardware review is finished (11 November 2026: docs/hardware-review, and the Other computers page, site/hardware.html). It says: buy a fanless N150-class PC with a TPM (the OnLogic CL260 for a battery site, the Lenovo ThinkEdge where the brand matters), prove it on the bench with a cheap mini PC first, and keep the Verdin AM62 and the Luna out of the order book. The old Mallow trial was not to be run as written, and its page is now the side-by-side trial, for whichever computer is picked: the Verdin AM62 Quad now lists at US$306 (not US$107), the heatsink on its list does not fit, 'half a Pi 4' was never measured, and Torizon with a privileged container is the hardest stack to get approved. RPi ALERT already runs unchanged off a Raspberry Pi. The builder's processor sums are corrected to RPi ALERT's own measurements, and the catalogue and builder carry the review's computers. A hardware-neutral firmware layer (firmware/: a package for Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04, a container and disk images) is started: as at 13 November 2026 the package is built and its own checks pass on Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 with stand-ins for the radio, the container has been tried with stand-ins on one PC only (not on Torizon OS or ARM), the disk images are still being written, nothing has been run with a real radio stick off a Raspberry Pi, and there is no release yet (firmware/README.md is the current word). A draft security pack for IT assessors is in docs/security, with SECURITY.md. Prices re-checked in November 2026: each part is what one costs from an Australian shop with it in stock (else the cheapest way to get one, and when), and every bill — configurator, builder, trial — adds each shop's delivery once and clearance on an overseas order over A$1,000. The Pi 5 4 GB is A$249 in stock (A$178 was a back-order price); the RFI COL54 collinear is A$3,218 at Techwave, not the A$650 guessed; the RTL-SDR Blog V4 is end of life, so the V3 is the builder's stick. The builder and the side-by-side trial rate every computer for the whole computer and for one core, on RPi ALERT's decoders. The review was checked against its sources again on 13 November 2026: the Lenovo ThinkEdge's Ubuntu and Red Hat certification is Lenovo's own statement (Canonical's public list did not show it), nobody has checked that the package installs on Moxa's Secure system, and the configurator now counts channels from the corrected sums (a Pi 4 carries about five with room to spare, a Pi 3B+ two).
next: Check the review's prices and links by hand in a browser (Core Electronics, PB Tech, element14, Arrow, Toradex direct): the links matter more than the figures

Ask Lenovo for the ThinkEdge SE10n Gen2's Ubuntu certificate and which release it covers, and what its 0.7 m/s air-flow rating means in a closed cabinet; ask Moxa or its seller whether Moxa Industrial Linux 4 Secure takes Node.js and rtl-sdr from Debian's packages
Switch on private vulnerability reporting in this repository's and RPi ALERT's settings, and confirm or change the support period in docs/security/support.md
Review and release the RPi ALERT settings a managed network needs (docs/hardware-review/wip), then move firmware/PIN to that release
Check what is still marked est. with suppliers: the mating Bulgin lead, the earth kit, the 18 Ah battery, delivery from shops that price it only at checkout
Point the Quansheng V3 entry at quansheng_alert_ALL's browser installer
Re-check the FW-LAB entry: Flood-Net's runbook says to retire and archive it
Set GitHub Pages to publish only from GitHub Actions: two jobs publish on every push (pages.yml and the branch build), and each lays the site out differently
later: Recalibrate the builder's CPU model once RPi ALERT runs on a CM5 or a Verdin AM62, and once filtering around bursts passes a check at the first base station
Write the open-ALERT ALERT1 encoder firmware (catalogued as planned)
Write the open-ALERT store-and-forward repeater on RPi ALERT's receive side
Re-check quote-only and estimated prices with suppliers
now: Run the package on a real computer with a real radio stick, and the benchmark in firmware/bench on a Pi 4 and an N100 or N150 mini PC: nothing has yet been run off a Raspberry Pi, and every speed figure is a stand-in
Finish firmware/: try the container on Torizon OS and on an ARM computer, the disk images, the automatic build, then a first release

components.name: Rules engine
components.what: Needs → requirements → per-slot fit → supporting parts → power, cost and consequences.

components.name: Hardware catalogue
components.what: 263 parts in six family files, each with price and its source, power, temperature, grade, openness and sources.

components.name: ALERT equipment and software
components.what: ERT-A2, Campbell and HSE units, encoders and base-station software — where the sibling repositories are cited.

components.name: Presets and example networks
components.what: 22 preset sites and 5 example networks as starting points; buyable ones must meet every must.

components.name: Configurator page
components.what: Configurator: Sites, Network, Parts catalogue and How it works, behind one menu shared by every page; state in localStorage and share links.

components.name: Base station builder
components.what: build.html: how a receiving base fits together, the stick planner and CPU model, the bill with price ranges, lead times and suppliers, the build steps, and when a board of your own is worth it.

components.name: Side-by-side trial
components.what: trial.html: a computer that is not a Raspberry Pi beside a Pi 4 on one antenna. Pick the computer (the default is an N150 mini PC); the page gives the benchmark to run first, every computer rated for your channels, a shopping list, the steps, and a results sheet with pass rules. It was the Mallow trial (a Verdin AM62 on Mallow) until the hardware review.

components.name: Network check
components.what: Adds sites up by quantity and checks field stations, repeaters and bases meet on protocol and path.

components.name: Tests
components.what: node --test: every record and reference, every preset, and the sizing, pricing and network rules.

components.name: Publishing
components.what: Deploys site/ to GitHub Pages on every push to main, only if the tests pass.

components.name: Hardware review
components.what: The review of the old Mallow trial and of which computer, other than a Raspberry Pi, should run a base station: the Other computers page, the README, the comparison tables, and thirteen research reports with three re-checks.

components.name: Base station package (firmware/)
components.what: RPi ALERT's signed release, unchanged, as a package for Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 (standard and enterprise profiles), with a benchmark. Its own checks pass on Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 with stand-ins for the radio (13 November 2026). The container has been tried with stand-ins for the radio on one PC only (not on Torizon OS or ARM); the disk images are still being written. Not yet run with a real radio stick off a Raspberry Pi; no release yet.

components.name: Security pack
components.what: What an IT assessor is handed: overview, shared responsibility, controls, a proposed support period, and how to report a flaw. A draft.

components.name: open-ALERT encoder and repeater
components.what: An open ALERT1 encoder for a $10 board and a Pi store-and-forward repeater — catalogued, not written.

provides.name: ALERT hardware catalogue
provides.what: Plain-JavaScript records of 263 parts with prices and their sources, power, grades and links, for costing ALERT sites.

provides.name: open-ALERT configurator
provides.what: The page itself, and share links to a configured site or network.

provides.name: Base station builder
provides.what: A page for planning and building one ALERT receiving base station on RPi ALERT, from parts to readings in Flood-Net.

provides.name: Side-by-side trial plan
provides.what: What to buy and do to test a computer that is not a Raspberry Pi running RPi ALERT beside a Pi, and how to judge it. (The id is kept from when it was the Mallow trial, so links to it still hold.)

consumes.what: The DP32G030 UV-K5 entry: archived but flashable, read through a K-plug cable at 38,400 baud.
consumes.on_change: Update quansheng-uv-k5-dp32 in site/data/radio.js; run npm test.

consumes.what: ALERT frame formats (ABF, EIF, framing, CRC) cited for the planned open encoder.

consumes.what: ALERT2 transition plan planning prices, ALERT1 tones and timing, the Serial Monitor entry, and Flood-Net as the destination (HTTPS, MQTT, HFEM, 115E-2-A2 bridge).
consumes.on_change: Update the PLAN-priced records in site/data/alert.js and site/data/site.js (and usdPerAud in site/js/engine.js), the floodnet-serial-monitor record, and the Flood-Net outputs in engine.js; run npm test.

consumes.what: The builder's stick windows, channel costs, burst cost and install routes: RPi ALERT's hardware notes, how it works, its installer and its SDR worker. The side-by-side trial follows its configuration (receiver ids, channels) the same way.
consumes.on_change: Re-check model.windows (each window's Pi 4 figure), loadFactor, the decoders' burstS and a2S, a2DecodeS and kioskCore in site/data/builder.js, the channel rule in site/js/engine.js (SDR_CH_CORE) and the steps() text in site/js/builder.js; run npm test.
